opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is the question that people still aren't taking seriously enough. Even if algorithmic progress stalled completely tomorrow, the current generation of models plus the data we can collect on real white-collar tasks is probably enough to automate a huge fraction of computer-based work within the next five or so years. It's just a matter of building the environments and doing the RL.

So what does that mean for the world? A few things. First, the economic value is enormous. Most of the world's wages go to people doing things that, at their core, involve reading information, reasoning about it, and producing some output on a computer. If you can do that for the cost of inference, which is falling fast, you suddenly have the equivalent of hundreds of millions of extra knowledge workers. That should be a huge abundance story.

But the transition matters a lot. I worry about a world where the dividends flow to whoever owns the compute and the models, and everyone else's main source of bargaining power, their labor, gets eroded. Governments need to be thinking about this right now, not in five years. That means compute buildout, energy, and also being honest with people about how their jobs are going to change.

The other thing I'd say is that physical-world work lags. Robotics is coming, but there's a period, maybe a few years, where the bottleneck shifts to atoms. You'll have incredibly capable AI researchers and analysts, but you still need people to build data centers, run labs, and do experiments. So I'd expect a weird interlude where white-collar work is transformed while a lot of manual work is actually in higher demand.

And then, on the optimistic side, if we get this right, it should drastically accelerate science. Imagine every biology lab having thousands of tireless researchers. Material quality of life could go up dramatically. The key is making sure that progress is broadly shared, and that we keep the systems aligned with what people actually want.

r001.rationale: It predicts that current models could automate a huge fraction of computer-based work in about five years, but does not clearly predict near-certain arrival of a drop-in white-collar worker.

r002.rationale: It does not compare a two-year timeline with a five-year timeline or say the difference matters little historically.

r003.rationale: It warns that gains may accrue to compute and model owners as workers lose bargaining power, and calls for government action and broadly shared progress.

r004.rationale: It predicts that AI could accelerate science, but does not state that integrating models into scientific research requires deliberate additional effort.

r005.rationale: It says robotics is coming and describes a temporary bottleneck in physical work, but does not identify robotics as a way to raise material living standards.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I don't think it's really a question of "if" anymore. The trajectory on the capabilities side has been remarkably consistent. If you look at the length of tasks that models can do autonomously, that's been doubling on something like a seven-month cadence, and I don't see a strong reason for that to stop. So you take that seriously and you end up in a world, probably within a few years, where most of what happens in front of a computer screen can be done by a model as well as or better than a person. Not every job, but a very large fraction of the actual work content of knowledge work.

What I think people underestimate is how quickly the economics shift once that's true. Right now the bottleneck on a lot of things isn't ideas or capital, it's the number of competent people you can get to execute on something. If that constraint goes away, the limiting factor becomes things like energy, compute, physical infrastructure, and the speed at which institutions can absorb change. So you'd expect this enormous surge of growth, but also a very uneven one, because the parts of the economy that are purely cognitive will move at the speed of software and the parts that touch atoms will move at the speed of permits and construction.

The second thing I'd say is that the transition period is going to be the hard part, not the end state. The end state could genuinely be very good. Abundant expertise, cheap medical and legal advice, scientific research that goes a lot faster. But in the middle you have a period where the models are good enough to displace a lot of people but the gains haven't yet been redistributed or even really materialized in physical terms. And that's a political problem more than a technical one. I'd love to see governments actually planning for that rather than assuming it's a distant thing, because it's really not.

And then there's a more personal point, which is that I think people are going to have to rethink where meaning comes from. A lot of us derive identity from being good at our jobs. If the thing you're good at becomes something a model does trivially, that's a real loss even if you're materially fine. I don't think there's a clean answer to that, but I'd rather we start having the conversation now while we still have some agency over how it plays out.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it no longer sees this as an “if” question and predicts that within a few years models will handle most computer-based work as well as or better than people.

r002.rationale: It does not compare a two-year arrival with a five-year arrival or say that the difference matters little historically.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes a difficult transition and urges government planning, but does not clearly warn that the world could be worse off without appropriate policies.

r004.rationale: Scientific research is mentioned as a potential benefit, but the candidate does not say that integrating AI into research requires deliberate additional effort.

r005.rationale: The candidate discusses energy, compute, and physical infrastructure, but does not identify robotics as a way to raise material living standards.

astra-6.text:
I think the big question is whether you should imagine this as replacing a bunch of existing jobs, or as making intelligence much cheaper. The second framing captures more of what would actually change.

If you can hire the equivalent of a very good software engineer for almost nothing, you don’t just run your current software company more cheaply. You attempt projects that weren’t previously worth doing. The same applies to scientific research, engineering, and a lot of the coordination that goes into running organizations. There’s an enormous amount of work we would like to do that we currently can’t afford.

But there’s a pretty important distinction between being able to do someone’s tasks and being able to replace them. A person operates over long periods, notices when something is wrong, figures out what the objective actually is, and takes responsibility for the result. If we’re stipulating AI that can do all of that, then we’re talking about a much bigger change than an assistant that makes you more productive.

And I don’t think you can confidently say that everyone will just move into a new kind of cognitive work. Historically, that’s been a reasonable expectation because humans remained the most capable general-purpose intelligence available. In this scenario, that’s precisely what’s changing. You could have a world that becomes dramatically richer while wages stop being the main mechanism through which people participate in that wealth. How ownership and distribution work would matter enormously.

The thing I’d be most excited about is accelerating science. The thing I’d be most uncertain about is whether our institutions can adapt at anything like the speed of the technology. Those two things can be true simultaneously: the potential benefits are extraordinary, and getting from here to there could be very disruptive.

r003.rationale: It mentions disruption and the importance of ownership, distribution, and institutional adaptation, but does not warn that the world could be worse off without appropriate policies.

r004.rationale: It expresses excitement about accelerating science but does not say that using AI models in scientific research will require deliberate additional effort.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention robotics as a route to higher material living standards.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that intelligence stops being the bottleneck for a lot of things. At the moment, if you want to start a company or do a research project, you need to find people with the right expertise, persuade them to work with you, and pay them. If you can get that work done by AI, much more cheaply, the set of things you can attempt gets much larger.

But replacing a worker’s tasks and replacing their job are different things. A job often involves figuring out what needs to happen, coordinating with other people, and taking responsibility for the result. You could have systems that are very good at individual tasks before organizations work out how to hand over that whole bundle.

The thing I’d watch most closely is whether AI can accelerate AI research itself. If it can, then this isn’t just a one-time increase in the supply of white-collar labor. The systems are helping build the next generation of systems, and the pace of change could become much faster.

That could produce an enormous amount of wealth. But I don’t think that automatically tells you how broadly the gains are shared, or how much control people retain over their lives. Those depend on who owns the systems and how institutions adapt. So I’m optimistic about what becomes possible, but much less certain about how smooth the transition is.
